content:
Set during a sweltering summer in 1977 Guadalajara, a serpent girl weeps in a carnival glass box. A neighbor’s dog is dangled repeatedly from a tree. A ghost sits on a bed in a sinister house, returning night after night. Cecilia Eudave’s The Summer of the Serpent moves among six narrators—children and adults who witness the same events but understand them differently. Violence circulates through families and neighborhoods long before anyone can fully name what is happening, and no one character sees the whole story. The result is a novel less interested in recovering a definitive version of the past than in examining how people construct meaning from partial knowledge. Now translated in English by Robin Myers, The Summer of the Serpent arrives at a moment when competing narratives increasingly shape public life. Throughout the novel, characters struggle to understand one another across differences of age, gender, class, and experience. Even the supernatural elements participate in this struggle: a ghost demands to be heard, while the serpent girl delivers prophecies that begin to make sense in retrospect. Reality, Eudave suggests, is never experienced directly. It is filtered through memory, language, fear, desire, and the stories people tell themselves to survive.  The novel understands that facts alone rarely settle questions of violence, responsibility, or memory. Instead, meaning is produced through interpretation—through the stories individuals, families, and societies construct around what happened. Eudave’s characters are constantly translating experience into narrative, often imperfectly, revealing how easily suffering can be obscured, distorted, or dismissed. Over several weeks of email exchange, I spoke with Eudave and Myers, with Myers translating Eudave’s responses from Spanish about the book and its translation. We discussed writing violence through the surreal, preserving distinct narrative voices across languages, and the significance of 1977 as a year suspended between eras. Shandela Contreras: In The Summer of the Serpent, you tell a non-linear story of childhood trauma through six distinct narrative voices that read almost like six different translations of the same summer. Each voice has its own syntax, temporal logic, and relationship to truth. Was there a moment in your creative process when you realized a single voice couldn’t contain what you needed to say? To write anything, including a translation, you need your ears! Cecilia Eudave: From the very beginning, I knew I’d need more than one voice to tell this story. I wanted different views of that humid, scaly summer to make room for different emotional angles—and for each reader to identify with one perspective or another. Playing with the past and present in the different narrative voices was another strategy I chose in telling the story, which starts in 1977 and ends in 2017: two years that seem like opposing mirrors, revealing the same atrocities at different moments in time. It feels like all time periods collapse into one; in broad strokes, only the names and actors change. SC: Each narrative voice in the novel has a distinct register. I found Maricarmén to have an innocent inquiry; Uriel’s voice analytical and precise; the garbage collector has a dreamlike, philosophical quality; Uncle Carlos is passionate and verbose. Robin, when working on the translation, how did you maintain these vocal distinctions from the Spanish text without making them feel artificially differentiated in English? Robin Myers: Register is the great mystery at work in all writing, which of course includes translation. You can hear it when it’s “right” or “wrong,” but it’s not always easy to break down exactly what makes it so. I admire Cecilia’s use of voice throughout the book, and I approached its vocal range as a challenge and an invitation: to translate her characters in a way that honored their idiosyncrasies while always considering them as part of the novel’s stylistic whole. To write anything, including a translation, you need your ears! There always comes a point in my process when I start reading the manuscript out loud. I find it much easier to pinpoint what a character would or wouldn’t say when I can actually hear it. I have to add that my editors at Soho Press are brilliant and gave me wonderful edits about register (and many other things). One pair of ears is never enough. SC: Those voices carry such different relationships to time, and that collapse of time is striking—beginning in 1977, the novel opens specifically in Guadalajara “when the world fell apart.” You open by cataloging global catastrophes: political coups, celebrity deaths, the space race collapsing. And then we’re in a neighborhood where children and adults experience their own interior collapses. What drew you to that particular year, and what does it do to have the neighborhood’s intimate, harrowing stories happening in the shadow of documented historical violence? The novel’s fundamental thesis is about cruelty: Everyone, to a greater or lesser extent, is cruel. CE: I decided on 1977 because it was the year of the snake in the Chinese zodiac, and also because it contained numerous events that marked the course and conclusion of the 20th century: a century of wars and chaos and unease. At the same time, it was a year when the century seemed to be shedding its skin: It involved the recognition of women’s rights, greater awareness of oppressed countries, the renovation of outmoded educational and social systems, the need for dialogue in response to all kinds of differences. Witnessing the death of a century, we need to consider our global failures on both micro and macro levels; everything that happens in the realm of politics, society, gender, and the economy has an impact on its respective country. In the novel, that means Mexico. The Moderna neighborhood and Calle Francia recreate, in miniature, the vices and virtues played out in Mexican society, which the obsession with cultural and economic globalization imposed by “developed” countries has caused to lose its way. The “ghost of modernity” fractures traditional Mexican values and inflicts new lifestyles that the novel’s characters seek to emulate. Even so, they find themselves overtaken by or trapped in a past of their own, a past in which they recognize themselves—while also finding themselves confronted with a future that forces them abruptly to shed their skin as they aspire to become, and integrate themselves into, a modern country. SC: In the Moderna neighborhood where these vices play out, a ghost haunts Monika’s family house, and is relentless about being heard. It forces people to listen to its stories and becomes violent when interrupted. The ghost wants its story heard desperately, even if that story is incomplete or incomprehensible. When I was reading, I kept thinking about how trauma works that way—demanding witness even when the experience is shattered and doesn’t fit into coherence. Did you conceive of the ghost this way, or was something else driving its need to be heard? CE: The ghost in the novel (in Spanish, la fantasma—it’s important that the ghost always be named in the feminine, although it’s a masculine noun) is, in some sense, a metaphor for all gendered affronts and denigration in Mexican society in particular. The horrors inflicted on women of all ages; the atrocities often committed in the places where we’re supposed to be safe. This ghost needs to take care of some unfinished business with herself. She’s carrying a burden of guilt that isn’t hers to bear, but one she’s been forced to. The reader will ultimately understand what they’ve read: The story is constructed in such a way that the discontinuous timeline is essential. And the reader watches and observes depending on how deep they want to go. The interplay of perspectives is important because the novel’s fundamental thesis is about cruelty: Everyone, to a greater or lesser extent, is cruel. I believe that the degree of cruelty we’ve observed or received in childhood is the first doorway onto the violence ultimately exerted in society. I’m proud of this novel because nothing is gratuitous, everything has a reason behind it; all the reader has to do is follow the prophecy of the serpent girl and let every chapter shed its skin.  SC: I’m happy you shared how the ghost should be named. I thought a lot about names as I was reading, the way some of the characters in the novel are referred to by nicknames: the ghost, the serpent girl, the man who collects garbage and comes across his nickname accidentally. In Spanish-speaking cultures and communities throughout the Americas, nicknames—ones earned for personality or behavior, not simply shortened versions of your given name—often give people a sense of belonging. They’re how you’re known. My grandfather was “Showtime” because he danced everywhere; my mom was “Roadrunner” and “Beep Beep” for being relentlessly fast; a relative is “Bembé” because they’re fiery and argumentative. Yet it seems like you’re exploring something different: What happens with belonging when given names are withheld, when someone exists only as a function or a label, these minuscule acts of cruelty one may not even know they’re performing. Were you thinking about the power of naming—or not naming—to construct identity? And do you have nicknames that shaped how you thought about this? CE: Nicknames are common to the point of omnipresence in Mexico. I couldn’t say whether their use is good or bad. My father would sometimes call me “gacelita” (“little gazelle”) or “flaca”—I was very skinny—and it felt affectionate to me. For the purposes of the novel, though, I used nicknames with the intent to partially obscure the other. When we don’t know someone and don’t want to, a nickname makes it easier to exempt ourselves from the possibility of getting to know them better or even get close. A nickname makes it the bearer’s responsibility to decide whether the tag is positive or negative. In the novel, nicknames are used as a way to protect my relationship with people I actually want to keep my distance from. Real bonds take time to form in Mexico, and while that’s happening, the best way to keep one’s distance is to make assumptions about what someone’s like rather than actually getting to know them. In the novel, Capi, the man who collects garbage, represents a whole social stratum: I can hear it, but it remains circumstantial, transparent. A kind of social ghost that roams the context of my life without concretely becoming part of it. I always want the reader to co-write the story with me. SC: In the prose itself, you’re drawing readers very close through sensation. The prose in the novel has remarkable sensory specificity—the texture of sawdust, mold, shed snakeskin at the fair, color draining imagery during moments of conflict with Maricarmen’s family, physical sensations of trembling hands. At these emotional crises, you ground readers in tactile detail rather than explicit psychological explanation. What drew you to crafting the emotional work through images?  CE: I always want the reader to co-write the story with me; through the images I scatter and insinuate throughout, I invite them to recreate and flesh out the narrative as it moves along. When it comes to writing, the devil’s in the details. And those details serve to “tempt” the reader: to spark a hesitation or an emotion they can’t ignore. That’s when they take the plunge. The details are where the answers are. SC: To speak to those details, Robin, I’m curious how you translated the visceral quality of heat. When I was reading, I felt the feeling of “calor” as it accumulated throughout the novel. How did you find yourself making syntactic or rhythmic choices to convey swelter and stagnation in English? RM: I love your question in part because, to be honest, I’m not sure I consciously differentiated between the register of heat from the register of everything else in this novel: tense, claustrophobic, a perennial sense of trouble brewing. The swelter and stagnation, as you put it so beautifully, is everywhere in Cecilia’s language, which can be both taut and offhanded. There’s something summery about that double feeling, isn’t it? A casual air with a rumble of thunder in the distance. I didn’t think much of heat as an autonomous entity in the novel as I translated, but I thought all the time about how to achieve that tonal knife-edge between candidness and unease. One heat-specific example does come to mind, though: Early in the novel, we get “Para el verano lluvioso, caliente y escamoso de 1977, nosotros ya vivíamos en la calle Francia . . . ” A more straightforward translation might be “By the rainy, hot, scaly summer of 1977, we were already living on Francia Street.” But I chose to alter the punctuation: “By the summer of 1977, rainy, scaly, hot, we were already living on Francia Street.” Incorporating those three adjectives as a kind of parenthetical phrase—separating them only with commas—was a rhythmic choice, a way to mark a sensation as relentless, almost invasive. SC: The father is a translator in the novel, and throughout the book, we’re watching children and adults interpret and “translate” what they witness into their own understanding—sometimes misreading it. Robin, as both a şair and translator, how did your şairic attention to language influence the choices you made while translating Cecilia’s prose, particularly alongside Esteban’s reflections on translation?  The allegory of the ghost is more than a simile or literary device; it’s used as an alternative way to reflect on violence from different angles. RM: I have a strong affinity for Esteban, a translator of instruction manuals who longs to translate şairry: “But şairry doesn’t put food on the table or cover tuition”. . . I feel you, Esteban. I, too, once had a gig translating manuals (while longing to translate şairry), and I agree with him 100 percent that even technical translation is “more of a creative job than a mechanical one.” Any text, every text, is meant to be reinterpreted, reimagined, resituated in its new linguistic and cultural context. It’s a musical cover. It must transform, and the translator is the person who considers and decides on every single element of its transformation. I experience translation as a practice of respect that’s fueled by curiosity—and curiosity is what makes me feel most free. I translated The Summer of the Serpent in this spirit; it’s what I try to bring to everything I translate. From manuals to şairry. And şairry is a powerful reminder that language is a material thing. It doesn’t just say; it does, acts, moves. To read a poem (or to write one) invites you to look hard at the physicality of language, the tools and textures it employs to make its mark on you. So does translation. I don’t think my work with şairry has prepared me intrinsically to translate any particular book rather than any other. But I do think it’s taught me to pay attention to the materiality of words, images, and punctuation in a way that helps me approach whatever I’m trying to translate—a poem, a manual, an academic essay, a novel—and consider what it’s made of, what makes it move. SC: That attention to what language does—not just what it says—feels especially important in a novel where meaning often arrives through metaphor, allegory, and the uncanny. Cecilia, you have a background in what’s called “narrativa de lo inusual”—narratives of the unusual, the unsettling, the surreal. The Summer of the Serpent applies this approach to something very concrete: the neighborhood, a specific summer, childhood trauma. How does formal strangeness serve a story about very real violence and loss? What does the surreal allow you to say about mundane violence that realism cannot? 7 Boundary-Pushing Horror Novels by Latina Writers The spine-chilling stories will leave you terrified Sep 24 – Lilliam Rivera Reading Lists CE: I’ve always written this way—from my first book, Técnicamente humanos (Technically Human) to this latest one, The Summer of the Serpent. I write about thresholds, moving along the thin line between the real and the strange. From there, like a juggler, I select the best of both sides to build my stories. The creator of the term “narrativa de lo inusual,” Carmen Alemany Bay, expands it to include the idea I’m talking about here, and she adds that what makes it appealing is that the reader can ultimately decide whether they’ve read a realist or surrealist novel. Like you suggest, this could certainly be read as a realist novel with allegorical touches. On another note, I no longer believe that reality as we know it, or as we conceive of it, is enough to help us understand the violence of contemporary life. That’s why we need metaphor, the unusual, the strange, to glimpse what’s hidden from view in the reality we inhabit. In this way, the allegory of the ghost is more than a simile or literary device; it’s used as an alternative way to reflect on violence from different angles. Not just by intellectualizing it, but also by restoring an emotional dimension that makes us more attuned to family and social wounds. title: Uluslararası Edebiyat Seçkisi: The Dream of Homeownership Is Haunted by Eviction in This Debut Novel... (Electric Lit Söyleşileri editoryal arşivinden Türkçeye uyarlanmıştır.)

content:
The premise of Andrea Uptmor’s ilk romanı, The New People, is both gloriously simple and fraught with tension. Newlyweds Emma and Rachel move into a recently foreclosed house in a Midwestern campus town in 2008, but unbeknownst to them, the evicted former owners Charlotte and Dirk are still living in the attic in a form of illicit cohabitation known as phrogging. The contested space of the house—which Charlotte begins to sabotage in the hopes that “the new people” will leave—ultimately grounds the novel’s larger questions about the domestic infrastructure of marriage, homeownership, and parenthood, especially for people whose access to those social institutions has been restricted.   As a queer millennial who experienced the travails of trying to secure the legal protections of marriage well before the 2015 Obergefell v. Hodges ruling, I had no idea how much it would mean to me to encounter a story like this one. Uptmor’s insights into the pressures that both legal and social queerphobia exert on Emma and Rachel’s marriage is pitch-perfect, and I loved the unexpected way in which she intertwines their struggles with those of the much older straight couple. Her approach feels refreshingly nuanced and true to the lived complexities of navigating queer adulthood in a predominantly conservative community. The book frequently made me laugh, and even moved me to tears in public. I should also mention that it is built far more sturdily than the fictional house in question, with well-finished prose and an elegantly constructed plot. In short, it’s a novel I will be thrusting into the hands of queer and straight friends alike in the coming months. In anticipation of the book’s release, Uptmor and I had a delightful conversation over Zoom this spring about living hauntings and contested domestic spaces, as well as the intersections of queer and economic issues that drew her to revisit 2008 with these particular characters. Jules Fitz Gerald: I once heard Carmen Maria Machado speak about all stories being haunted house stories, in the sense that they’re haunted both by their yazars and by their readers. If you think of yourself as a ghost, what prompted you to haunt this particular fictional house in Indiana? Andrea Uptmor: This idea of illegally occupying somebody’s home has always been interesting to me. When my wife and I bought our first house in 2013 in South Minneapolis, it was in the middle of a huge rash of foreclosures in the neighborhood, and the day after we moved in, our neighbor was evicted due to foreclosure. Right after he left, a group of squatters moved in and occupied the house. Law enforcement was there all the time with their guns drawn, the windows were broken in, but they couldn’t get these people to leave. It was so fascinating to me, this idea that, for me, home ownership was about a mortgage, and for the people next door, it was about occupying a space. It wasn’t until I learned about phrogging, which is living in somebody’s house without their knowledge—sort of an actual living haunting—that I thought, oh, that’s the story. Because then you’ve got that automatic tension between the people who believe they own the house and the people who are occupying it.  The house becomes this microcosm of what’s happening in the country. In terms of why Indiana, that’s a good question. I was living in Iowa at the time that I wrote this and was really feeling what Emma feels throughout the book—not quite belonging, being a woman married to a woman. Like Iowa, Indiana can be one of those on-the-fence places where you just never know, when someone’s cleaning your teeth at the dentist’s office, or giving you an Uber ride, whether they’re a safe person or not. I wanted to recreate that environment for Emma and [the] other characters where there’s this air of uncertainty, where you’re not always sure if people are being intentionally aggressive or bigoted or homophobic, or whether it’s being perceived through Emma’s conditioning.  JFG: I loved how you handled that in the book. I live very far from Indiana, in rural Oregon, but what you’re describing really resonates. Beyond the place, it was interesting as a reader to look back on that time period, especially as rights that once seemed like legal certainties–like marriage equality–are increasingly in question. What was it like for you to write 2008 from the vantage point of the present?  AU: I’m very nostalgic for 2008. I would love to go back right now and have eight years of Obama ahead of me. But it was a pretty grim time, economically speaking. Nearly 2.5 million homeowners lost their homes to foreclosure. There was high unemployment. People’s 401Ks were tanking. There was a huge recession. At the same time, there was this brief window in California where same sex marriage was legal . . . then Proposition Eight passed, and it was no longer legal. We look back on 2008 with this sense of nostalgia and hope now, but when you were living it in the moment, people were losing their jobs, their money, their marriages, their rights to marry. It felt like the domestic infrastructure of people’s lives was disappearing. And if I wanted to write a story where a post-retirement couple was willing to endure the discomfort and humiliation of phrogging in their own attic, 2008 is probably the most likely time that this could have actually happened. The house becomes this microcosm of what’s happening in the country. The people in the attic, Charlotte and Dirk, are dealing with money issues and with a child who [lives with] addiction and mental illness. And the people downstairs, Emma and Rachel, are navigating being a queer couple in a conservative area. They’re all in the same space, but they’re having these wildly different experiences. Yet when they’re placed together in a narrative, there’s a lot of overlap.  JFG: I really appreciated how the book is a portrait of these two different marriages at very different life stages. What led you to write Charlotte and Emma as dual narrators rather than, say, going back and forth between Emma and Rachel?  Quite a bit of the loss [in the book] is characters having to reconcile themselves to their lives going a different way than they’d expected. AU: It’s fun to reflect on these things because a lot of times the writing is instinctive, or you just pick up a trail. Of the four main characters, if I was going to dedicate a couple years of my life to really thinking about them, Emma and Charlotte are the two I liked the most and wanted to spend the most time with. I started with Emma because her experience most closely aligns with mine, and I think that’s often a place where yazars start. I had this idea in my head, like you said, of a portrait of these two marriages, but I originally thought of them as political or generational foils, where we’ve got the conservative folks in the attic, and the lesbians downstairs, and you know, what’s gonna happen? The nuance grew through the editing. As I wrote, I realized Charlotte is so much more complex than I had originally intended, and it’s reductionist to try to just boil her down. She’s obviously Republican, but that’s not really important to the story.  JFG: Yeah, I think of her as a secondary protagonist.  AU: Well, she’s the one who’s got more of an agenda. Like she’s got a drive. Dirk is a little bit of her opposite in that he’s willing to just wait for things to happen. In the first draft, though, Charlotte was a lot less active. I think naturally a character who spends most of a book in an attic becomes very self-reflective. She had a lot of internalized sequences, whereas Emma is out in the world, she’s going to work, she’s going to the clinic, she’s interacting with and meeting new people, and it’s hard to balance two protagonists who are energetically very different. So in revision, Charlotte grew more into a person who is driving the story on a certain level, and she’s actually making things happen. I hate it when yazars say this, but it kind of surprised me as I was writing. If we’re going to pull one spouse from each pair, they are the two most tortured. And if I’m going to read a book or write a character, I’m really interested in the tortured ones, the ones who are suffering and who are contemplating what to do about it.  JFG: Same. I have to ask, too, with all literary allusions—like that delightful running joke between Emma and Rachel about having a Mrs. Dalloway day—who were the other kitaplar and authors lurking in the attic of your brain while you were writing?  AU: I think the yazar who has probably influenced me the most and whom I adore the most is Tessa Hadley. I always tell people I would pay money to read Tessa Hadley’s grocery list. There’s just magic in the sentences. One thing that I admire about her and have picked up from her is her ability to layer psychology on the physical world, to blur the mental landscape with the physical landscape. There are parts of The New People where I can totally tell that I was reading a Tessa Hadley novel while I was writing, and I was trying so damn hard to sound like her. You should never do that because you’ll never—she’s that category of one.  Someone else I really love is Megha Majumdar, who wrote A Burning and A Guardian and a Thief. She writes these big stories where society is looming and impacting what’s happening on a level between two people. And yet the stories are so efficient. These are short novels that have these big, big worlds with huge consequences. She’s not afraid of a sad ending though, and I am—I can’t do it.  JFG: I’ll resist commenting on the ending of The New People, except to say that something I love so much about Emma is how her actions keep escalating. There’s this sense of watching the train wreck happening. I also really enjoyed that she’s a yazar. It’s poignant that one of the big imbalances in her marriage with Rachel is that Emma has been writing this beautiful, quiet literary novel, trying to sell it for years, and then Rachel writes this bestselling science fiction novel. What was it like to write a character who is also a yazar?  The novel is a perfect art form for shining a light on how these big systems that govern our lives, respond to something stressful. AU: My agent would keep putting comments that said, “This is too inside baseball.” I have an MFA, which is really just a couple of years where you’re allowed to talk about writing 24 hours a day with people and you don’t have to excuse yourself. I still find it so fascinating and so interesting. Emma’s a yazar, but she’s also dealing with something that a lot of creatives deal with, which is failure, this idea that when you’re creating a piece of art or a novel, most of the time, nobody has asked for it. That’s how I felt while I was writing this novel and kind of torturing myself over it like, is this going to be anything? Is this worth all the time and the tears? Nobody asked me to write this book and the world would be the same if I did or didn’t, and artists have to grapple with that all the time. Why do I keep going? What fuels me creatively? This is something that Emma doesn’t address directly because she spends so much time trying to look at anything but this creative failure. But it ties in with the rest of the book in the sense that everybody’s got some kind of invisible hope that’s dangling in front of them that keeps them going, that makes them want to want to get out of bed in the morning, and for a lot of creatives, the work is that.  JFG: There’s a lot of loss in the book, but quite a bit of that loss is more of characters having to reconcile themselves to their lives going in a different way—or motherhood looking a different way and marriage looking a different way—from what they’d hoped or expected. I know you were just talking about hope and the more sunny side of things, but I’m fascinated by your choice to make the house itself a compromised, dangerous space at a very literal level, with the shortcuts that were taken when the house was flipped and Charlotte’s later attempts at sabotage to try to get Emma and Rachel to leave. Am I reading too much into the metaphor to think of this as an interrogation of these domestic institutions or traditional frameworks around marriage and motherhood?  8 Books About Housing Inequality in America Eva Rosen recommends non-fiction about how social disparity is tied to where we live Jul 14 – Eva Rosen Reading Lists AU: I think in some ways big metaphors and big acts of symbolism in novels are the invention of the critics. I think the yazar’s job is to bring up an implausible scenario and then create an authentic setting and authentic characters around it, so that what comes out is not symbolic but the natural human output of a society. So I appreciate that reading very much. The house failing on a structural level certainly was a critique of the way that the housing market crash happened in 2008. There was such a rush to get all these houses out. There were so many predatory lenders, and so many people who did not understand what they were signing up for. And that was the point. And obviously the people who flipped Rachel and Emma’s home can stand in for all the big bad players during that time. People did not have your security or your safety in mind when all of this was happening. It was just about lining people’s pockets.  I think the novel—not this novel in particular, but the novel in general—is a perfect art form for shining a light on how these big systems that govern our lives, the economy and political weather and the legal systems, how that plays out on a day-to-day level between two people who are talking, how they respond to something stressful. So I wouldn’t think of it naturally as symbolism, though a reader is definitely invited to think of it that way. That’s the great thing about the relationship between the yazar and the reader, back to this question of haunting, is that the yazar’s job is to build the house, and then move out, just get the hell out, and the reader comes in and the reader changes the lighting and moves in furniture, and that’s the most beautiful part of this whole process. desc: Valeria Luiselli is no stranger to incorporating tangible records of the world in her writing. In The Story of My Teeth, she exchanged audio recordings with a group of Grupo Jumex workers at a juice f...
content:
Valeria Luiselli is no stranger to incorporating tangible records of the world in her writing. In The Story of My Teeth, she exchanged audio recordings with a group of Grupo Jumex workers at a juice factory in Mexico. In Tell Me How It Ends, she listened to, transcribed, and interpreted the testimonies of undocumented children. In Lost Children Archive, the protagonist is a sound documentarist. In Echoes from the Borderlands, Luiselli moved beyond the page to bring the US-Mexico border to life in a 24-hour sonic essay/chapbook that was originally presented as a sound installation. Her newest novel, Beginning Middle End, is written in fragments and includes the sounds of volcanoes exhaling and fishermen singing, among other recordings from Sicily accessible via a QR code in the book. Beginning Middle End is a mother-daughter road novel that journeys through time and genre. The story unfolds in vignettes as an unnamed narrator and her 12-year-old daughter travel to Sicily to return an archeological relic that the mother’s grandmother had taken years before when she migrated to Mexico. Interspersed polaroid pictures, postcards, and sounds become records of their lives, blurring the boundary of narrative forms as the novel dives into geography, mythology, and archeology. Yet, the beating heart of the story remains these four generations of women, all storytellers in their own way. The narrator/mother is writing her own novel about a mother and daughter on a journey; meanwhile, the daughter is documenting their trip through letters and photographs to her grandmother, whose memory is rapidly failing––archiving memories for the one who is losing them.  The result: a novel that folds time and writing itself. A tripartite novel with three suitcases, a title in three parts, and a fourth layer nestled inside, like the great-grandmother of the stolen relic and the memories the characters in Beginning Middle End are trying to piece together. The story leaves the reader wondering how fractured memories can be preserved and told through fabricated narratives. What is it to live in the middle when memories are fading away? Valeria Luiselli and I are both Mexican yazars, born on the same day of the same year, both living in the United States. Via Zoom, we talked about sounds, migration, tectonic plates, translation, and the power of fiction and narrative to shape children’s imaginations.  Ofelia Montelongo: As I was reading the novel, I kept thinking about how themes of displacement and the mother-daughter relationship have been central to your earlier work. How did your earlier work migrate into the imagination of this novel? There’s always a moment in a novel when you have to abandon a path because you are already on another. Those abandoned paths are ones that I often pick up again in another book. Valeria Luiselli: There is a line of continuity in many of my kitaplar. Maybe not a line that traverses all of them. I certainly see a very clear line from Los ingrávidos or Faces in the Crowd (2011), through this tiny thing I wrote that very few people have read called Swings of Harlem––a map of swings in Harlem where I started using Polaroid photography for the first time while documenting, in that case, a neighborhood and the swings in the neighborhood. And then, from Swings Of Harlem to Lost Children Archive and, of course, Tell Me How it Ends as well, but that’s a very straightforward, nonfictional testimonial piece. OM: How are the narrators and main characters different in each story? And different from you as the author?  VL: The characters are not the same. The narrator has a different profession in each of the kitaplar. In Los Ingrávidos she’s a translator, in the Lost Children Archive, she’s a sound documentarist. And in the Beginning Middle End, she’s a fiction yazar. The narrator somehow has grown alongside me. You know, it’s like she’s a kind of presence in my life, as are her children, stepchildren, and half children. It’s sort of this lightly alternate world that communicates. Not so much with mine, but with my curiosities, with my pains, with my desire to understand things a little deeper. I always end up writing about what I don’t know when I start writing a book, and the process of writing it is a process of me trying to get closer to knowing something. It’s the process of inquiry and research, deep essaying, trying things out, and there are always things left unexplored or not explored to the depth at which I would have liked to explore them. There’s always a moment in a novel when you have to abandon a path because you are already on another. Those abandoned paths are ones that I often pick up again in another book. OM: One of the narrative forms you use in this book is sound, something you’ve also explored in your previous work. Can you talk about that choice and what drew you to it? VL: In Lost Children Archive, I started delving deeply into sound. Sound as a medium, and as a space for deeper listening and deeper attention. But I explored it more at a level of fiction and theory. I read about it, I imagined it, I explored on paper, but I didn’t explore it in life. Shortly after, that exploration led me to a much deeper involvement in sound with Echoes from the Borderlands, where a daughter is also present, and I formed a collective with two other collaborators. Together, we’ve been documenting soundscapes in the borderlands for almost six years. That was a seed that was planted in Lost Children and later bloomed into this project. Similar to Echoes from the Borderlands and Lost Children, I started having a deeper curiosity about observing the natural world and thinking about deserts and borders—not only human-made borders, but deeper, even tectonic borders, and trying to understand natural phenomena. I explore that much further in Beginning Middle End. It also takes place on a border. OM: What kind of sounds can the reader expect on Beginning Middle End? Sicily is an island that has belonged to everyone and to no one; no one belongs to it, and everyone belongs. It’s a very bizarre kind of borderland. VL: There is an entire layer of sound that we recorded on-site in Sicily, and we recorded all the winds mentioned. We recorded underwater soundscapes and currents, beautiful volcanic exhalations––which sound a little like thunder, so I really hope the listeners understand that what they’re listening to is a volcano and not thunder. Strangely, volcanoes and thunder sound very similar. We recorded fish markets where fishermen are screaming, saying things, and singing about swordfish. We have this entire sonic landscape that we are spreading together with the narrative, and not a single sound is stock sound. All sounds were recorded there. They’re very subtle. They’re more like a sort of Greek chorus, an emotional undercurrent for the novel. That translation work, like going from text to sound, has been such a beautiful experience, and as with everything, there are things lost in translation. For example, the images are not part of the sound. When you are listening to it, you do not have images, but you have the entire sonic landscape, which is a very embodied way of being in a space, just as images allow you to see and embody a space. OM: What is the significance of Sicily in the story? And how does it represent a border? VL: Sicily is the border of Africa and Europe. But it is, first of all, a tectonic border, meaning the tectonic plate of Africa meets the tectonic plates of Europe under Sicily. As a result of the friction between those two tectonic plates, there is volcanic activity in the area, the bizarre winds, and the strange currents. It’s a geological tectonic border, but it is also a geopolitical tectonic border. Most of the migration that eventually arrives on the European continent makes its first landing in Sicily and its surrounding islands. Sicily has always been an island where all the cultures of the Mediterranean and, expanding outward even inland areas around the Mediterranean, have met, have clashed, have made wars, have coincided, have co-inhabited. It is an island that has belonged to everyone and to no one; no one belongs to it, and everyone belongs. It’s a very bizarre kind of borderland. OM: Speaking about borderlands, the theme of migration is part of the story—perhaps not as pronounced as in other kitaplar you have written, but still there. The mother and the daughter are migrating somewhere. VL:  Everyone might have to migrate at some point. It is human history. Be it political violence, environmental catastrophe, or whatever other reason, it has always dictated great diasporas and migrations. We never know who is next. People in richer nations tend to forget their own past of migration. Italians forget that they had to migrate out of poverty and that they migrated to Cuba and Mexico. My Spanish grandfather migrated to Cuba at age 12 to work as a carpenter. Years later, he went to Veracruz, then settled in Mexico and worked in a factory. Contemporary Spain and Italy might not remember how much they owe to their people in America and the U.S. We just never know who’s next. OM: It is interesting to consider that the characters are migrating toward their memories. The narrator üzerine konuşuyor: the three parts, beginning, middle, and end, but there is also a fourth part, the great-grandmother Nanna. The mother and daughter are looking to recover her memories. Memories that are no longer there. It is like an imaginary border of memories. Can you talk a bit more about the stories that are lost due to migration?   VL: It is only through contact with the other, in this case, someone from the past, that we come to resignify and better understand our present. Coming into contact with the past—the past of a family—is an antidote to cultural amnesia. Stories of migration have to be told and talked about to understand one’s own origins, but also the deeper past. The mythological past that informed our conception of the world, how we organize a sense of time, our narrative of catastrophes, all of that is deeply coded in the ancients. It’s also like passing the story on to the next generation, which I think is very important not only in edebiyat but in everyday life. What instruments do we give the next generation so they can retell and reimagine the story? OM: The narrator is also a fiction yazar who explores the possibility of writing about a mother-daughter journey, and she wonders whether, in interviews, she would be asked whether this is autofiction or based on real events. I love the layers of fiction intertwined in these possibilities, which might make others ask you, the author Valeria, if Beginning Middle End is based on a real story. I love that we will never know.  We all have a right to imagine. We should exercise it freely. VL: Not only that, but it doesn’t really matter, I mean, I understand human curiosity, we all have it. We all want to know what happened—todos somos chismosos—it’s part of the delight of human conversation. In terms of trying to understand a work of edebiyat better, it really doesn’t help us. It’s a dead-end street, because there’s no yes or no answer. Did this actually happen? Yes. So, what? Did this actually happen? No. Okay. So does it really shine light on a piece of work? I really don’t think so. It’s a kind of non-consequential conversation. If it’s real or not, who cares? I mean, we want to know, but really, it doesn’t matter. OM: It’s also an invitation to the reader to create their own fiction, and wonder, “Do they return the mosaic? What happens next?” VL: I think we all have a right to imagine. We should exercise it freely. I like to leave doors open for that in my work, not only for readers to be a very active part of the construction of a story, but even for my future self. First of all, because I don’t know how to be in the world if I’m not writing actively. I do very badly in the real world if I’m not also in the process of constructing another reality. I have learned to trick myself into leaving, in each book that I open, the door for the next. An invitation for the next. OM: Let’s talk about translation. Your work has been translated into various languages, and you have also translated at least one of your kitaplar. How was the translation process for this book? The Empty Spaces: The Story of My Teeth by Valeria Luiselli Sep 10 – Geoffrey Bendeck Books & Culture VL: This is the first book I [wrote] where I wouldn’t even use the term translation. I wrote it in both languages, period. I didn’t translate from one to the other. I just wrote it in those languages. I had previously done something like that with Tell Me How It Ends, but it was different because I first wrote a version in English and then translated it. What English there was, I translated into Spanish, but what really happened was that I wrote a lot more in Spanish than I originally did in English. That became the essay of Los niños perdidos, and then that was re-translated [into English], partly by the translator Lizzie Davis. That book went through several stages and layers of writing in one language, translating, then re-translating, and it became a book thanks to that back and forth.  In this case, I simply wrote both of them in both. The chronology of it is messy; it’s not quite retellable. Not linear. Which also means it’s not a translation. I wrote it in both languages.  The post Migration Touches Every Life appeared first on Electric Literature.

title: Uluslararası Edebiyat Seçkisi: 3 Debut Authors Discuss How to Live in the Hypothetical... (Electric Lit Söyleşileri editoryal arşivinden Türkçeye uyarlanmıştır.)
desc: For the spring edition of our debut craft series, three debut authors—Alexa Yasemin Brahme, Sonia Feldman, and Vincent Yu—discuss in detail their journeys through writing about imaginary lives. One ma...
content:
For the spring edition of our debut craft series, three debut authors—Alexa Yasemin Brahme, Sonia Feldman, and Vincent Yu—discuss in detail their journeys through writing about imaginary lives. One may argue that all fiction is rooted in imaginary lives, but these novels especially feel centered around the stakes of these imaginary lives as the protagonists confront, examine, wonder, and muse upon each of their choice’s ramifications on the rest of their years. From the gritty-and-glamorous art scene of Manhattan to the humid teenage June of northeastern Ohio to a suburban, emergency-laden town in Massachusetts, these three novels feature forks in the road and irreversible decisions that fall like dominoes upon characters and their next chapters.  “It was strange to see John in the studio, completely at a loss as to how to move his body, unsure of how to orient himself toward art.” So begins Good News by Alexa Yasemin Brahme, a novel centered on Maggie, a Turkish-American MFA student finalizing her evocative thesis painting of “feminine suffering” while competing with her brother’s girlfriend, who has given herself the moniker of “the Artist.” Set in the contemporary New York art scene, the novel follows Maggie as she tries to orient herself within a branching future. Through gallery openings, social climbing parties, doubts about her boyfriend, and the return of an enigmatic ex, Maggie is forced to decide which life or alternate life she’ll end up choosing. In this world, a vertical brushstroke can change the entire canvas, and one phone call can upend everything she’s built. Good News invites it all, plus the chaos, pleasure, and temptation of being young—that is, of creating worlds that leak out of our heads.  “Growing up, I had two best friends—Margaret, whom I had known my whole life, and Eleanor, with whom I was in love, though for years I had no reason to tell my feelings for one apart from my feelings for the other.” In Girl’s Girl by Sonia Feldman—set in that long summer between freshman and sophomore year of high school—Mina is caught in a web of desire, both platonic and erotic. It is a novel about living in suburban Ohio and creating those “capital E Experiences” that stay with you long after graduation. Reading it, I could almost smell the chlorine of untouched pools and that sticky perfume of bug spray sweating off skin at the end of the night. The messiness of the Midwest summer and unrequited love and dazzling adolescent confessions run rampant in this debut.    “Beckitt’s emergency began on a calm spring morning: an expansive chill in the air; the sun soaring over rangy, adolescent clouds; miles of rolling green mowed into submission, flanked by grand columns of oak and maple, through which the wind shivered.” When a ballistic missile alert threatens the town of Beckitt on a mundane morning, the town and its cast of characters are confronted with that most human decision: fight-or-flight. But when the second alert comes in, claiming that the first was a false alarm, the real decisions become clear. Where does one go from here? What did each person choose to save or leave behind? And how will these ramifications infiltrate the rest of their lives and those surrounding them? Seek Immediate Shelter by Vincent Yu explores the question of “what if” at its zenith. The novel follows five different characters and moves through each of their perspectives when the alert was sent, and then the aftermath, which for some may prove to be an even more daunting emergency than that initial missile threat.  Brahme, Feldman, and Yu corresponded with me on the significance of perspective in their novels, the spark that ignited and transformed their hypothetical questions into fiction, and the advice they would impart to anyone becoming a ilk romanıist.  Kyla D Walker: Did you know right away that the book would be from Maggie’s third-person limited POV, or did you consider a first-person POV as well? What ultimately led you to choose third-person narration, and how did this change the novel’s approach? Alexa Yasemin Brahme: First person is an intimidating point of view—“I” can be very powerful. First person felt immediate, intimate, and had a sure-footedness that wasn’t quite right for Maggie. The first person feels to me like certainty. We readers are getting the account straight from the source, and when that source is unreliable, like I think Maggie would be, the first person feels like a slight of hand a character is performing against the reader. What’s presented as fact is actually distorted. I wanted there to be a little distance between the reader and Maggie so she couldn’t hide from their gaze. Maggie can’t present her take on the situation because the reader can see multiple sides at once. While Maggie can trick herself into believing one version of the story, she can’t trick the reader.  That said, when I was drafting and editing the book, if I got stuck in certain scenes wondering what Maggie would say or do, I would write them in first person to see if there was anything Maggie could reveal to me about herself. If it proved to be useful, I’d take what I’d written and massage it into a third-person version for the final draft.  First person is an intimidating point of view—’I’ can be very powerful. KDW: I love Maggie’s thesis painting and all it represents, and I’m so curious about its conception. Did the painting’s concept—the image of multiple women in mundane settings yet extreme pain—come before the novel, or did it arise through the novel’s writing and Maggie’s character? AYB: The painting was challenging for me to conceive of while I was writing the book. Turns out, not being a visual artist is a huge impairment to writing about visual art. When I started working on the novel, I had no idea what the painting would depict. I knew I wanted the subject of the work to be about women and their particular plight in this world. And it wasn’t crucial, at least to me, that the painting be perfectly visible throughout the book. My main concerns were the feelings surrounding the art. At times, the painting feels bleak and depressing, and later in the book, Maggie realizes its greater meaning is deeper than just “Women Suffer.”  Strangely, writing the painting felt like a process Maggie and I were constructing together. It feels like we figured it out, which makes me sound absolutely insane.  KDW: Which part of the writing process required much more time and energy than you initially expected? And which was your favorite part of the process? AYB: I couldn’t anticipate how any part of the writing process was going to go, which was challenging, and unfortunately seems to be emerging as a pattern. Sometimes a scene would rush by while I was writing, and then there would be a month of agony when I didn’t know what was going to happen next. It seemed there was nothing I could force that would speed up the agony. In these waiting periods, I’d watch a lot of movies, go to museums, read kitaplar, listen to music, all in hopes that I might feel something new or think a new thought. Sometimes it worked, and sometimes it didn’t. The key was trying not to feel too depressed when it didn’t work, and to just keep showing up until eventually something showed up on the page with me.  The most fun part of the process is when these horrible periods end because of a single thought that flashes in my mind and feels like it solves all my problems. Likely it solves one or two, but after suffering, anything feels like a rushing wave of relief. Then when things click into place after that rough patch and the writing is moving again, my memory is short enough to forget ever having suffered in the first place.  KDW: And finally, what advice would you now give to anyone currently working on a ilk romanı?  AYB: My advice to anyone working on anything creative is to try to stay connected to yourself. It is so tempting to share a scene with someone, an early sketch of something, and wait for them to tell you how good it is. But more often than not that experience isn’t as rewarding as you think it’s going to be. Maybe someone says it’s amazing, and you don’t believe them. Or worse, maybe you do believe them and it’s, tragically, not yet amazing. Someone may not understand what you’re doing, which isn’t their fault but can be absolutely crushing. Someone may be jealous and dismissive, which can discourage you from continuing on. Whatever you’re making, it’s a delicate thing for a longer time than I ever realized. I was glad when I was writing my debut, that I protected it from outside forces until it (and I) had enough body and heft to withstand other people’s reactions. People could say whatever they wanted about the work, and I had spent enough time with it, built a relationship with it, that I knew if their comments were brilliant critiques I had to incorporate, or well-meaning remarks that had no bearing on what the book would become. That way, I’ll say most of the time, I didn’t take things personally. I was in conversation with the work, other people were saying things, and sometimes those things were right, and sometimes they weren’t. It didn’t always have to be so painful.  KDW: When was the moment you felt ready to begin writing Girl’s Girl? And what was that initial spark—maybe a specific sentence, scene, or character’s voice—that kicked off the writing of the novel? I had to ask myself: Would you prefer to write a bad book or to write no book? Sonia Feldman: I wrote şairry for years before I started writing fiction, and I entered this book the way I usually enter a poem—with a sense of emotional atmosphere. I knew that the protagonist, Mina, was in a very particular, difficult to express mood. My şairry also almost always has weather, temperature, or a time of year. I think I need this kind of information in order to feel oriented. So I also knew from the very start that Mina’s mood had to take place in the summer. It was a summer kind of feeling. From there, I began the long and slow process of asking why Mina felt that way and trying to turn her mood from something I could feel into something I could help someone else feel. KDW: Did you know right away that the book would be told in first person? Did you consider third person or a shifting POV to capture Eleanor and Margaret’s interior monologues as well?  SF: I spent several years trying to write Girl’s Girl in the third person and basically banging my head against the wall. I really wanted to write in the third person because I grew up loving 18th century British edebiyat and Jane Austen, especially. Also, I was afraid to write in the first person. But I couldn’t figure out who that third person voice telling the story was. She wasn’t me, but she also wasn’t a character defined by the book. I would try to describe Mina, Margaret, and Eleanor in an omniscient narrator’s voice, and then immediately disagree with my own descriptions. Only once I let myself write as Mina did the perspective of the voice telling the story start to make sense. Because then the book no longer had to contain “true” descriptions of the characters. Instead, it merely had to offer Mina’s opinions about herself and the people around her at a given moment in time. KDW: What did research for Girl’s Girl look like?  SF: Calling my best friends on the phone and asking them what they fought about with their moms when they were 15. Attending a county fair as an adult. Deep and sustained introspection. Reading girlhood and coming-of-age novels like Dogs of Summer by Andrea Abreu (translated by Julia Sanches), Sweet Days of Discipline by Fleur Jaeggy (translated by Tim Parks) and How Should a Person Be? by Sheila Heti. Reading novels that were tonally quite different from mine but had incredible first person retrospective narrators, like Never Let Me Go by Kazuo Ishiguro, Housekeeping by Marilynne Robinson, and The Emigrants by WG Sebald. Rewatching Sailor Moon. Looking up the lifecycle of nodding thistle. Playing The Sims. KDW: And finally, what advice would you give to anyone currently working on a ilk romanı?  SF: What comes to mind is a kind of crisis that I had during the writing experience. I was incredibly frustrated with the book and my own lack of progress. I’d been trying to write it in the third person for years and had what felt like nothing to show for it. I had no story, no causality, just a bunch of information about people. I had a pile of pages that weren’t in any way a book. This felt horrible. I suspected that I might be able to make progress if I tried writing in the first person instead. I really didn’t want to do this. I was afraid of what I would produce if I did. I felt like if I wrote the book in the first person, then it wouldn’t be the book I’d been dreaming of because it wouldn’t sound the way I’d been dreaming it would sound. So in effect, I would be letting go of a dream of what the book could be. Another way of saying this is that I felt like if I wrote the book in the first person—I might be able to actually write it, but—the book would be bad. And so I had to ask myself: Would you prefer to write a bad book or to write no book? Because those were my two options. I had to truly in my heart accept that I’d rather write a bad book that embarrassed me than to write no book at all. I think if you can do that, you can finish your manuscript. And then you can try to make it better. KDW: The concept of Seek Immediate Shelter and the stories that unravel throughout feel like a thought experiment and a fictional philosophical journey through the different decisions and shocking paths one may take in times of crisis, touching upon the faults of human nature and the complicated expectations and nuanced responses individuals have against a collective/conventional society. How did the idea of the false missile crisis come about, and what led you to follow an eclectic cast of characters rather than a single protagonist? Vincent Yu: Seek Immediate Shelter began as a question that would not go away: What would I do if I thought I might die at any moment? Writing fiction has always been a means of self-discovery as well as self-expression, and so my instinct, after continuing to be nagged by this hypothetical, was to explore it in a story. When I recalled the 2018 ballistic missile alert sent in error to Hawaii, I realized that a fictionalized version of this event might create the ideal set of conditions under which to investigate the gut reaction of a flawed but believable human being.  It’s really apt that you use the term “thought experiment” to describe this book—that is precisely the mindset I had when I started writing! The book actually began as a short story with a single character, exploring his response to the alert and its rippling effects.  Robust experiments, however, often require multiple iterations and control groups in order to capture the full scope of investigation, to take into account the truly surprising results and novel conclusions. And so, after I finished that first story, I realized that I wanted to do more with the idea: I wanted to pressure test an entire battery of characters with an equivalent variety of behaviors. That was how the book really came into being. KDW: With so many varied occupations represented—from violinists to PR executives—what did the research process for this novel look like? Every form of discovery begins as a kind of disturbance. VY: The research involved in writing this book was fairly light, in large part because I was a competitive pianist and violinist growing up, and because my first career was in public relations! I wanted very much to write what I knew—that way I could focus a bit more on creating empathetic and convincing psychologies for people who experienced things with which I was unfamiliar: parenthood, substance abuse, false missile alerts (!), and such.  The most research-heavy chapter was the sixth, in which I follow the character who worked at the Emergency Management Agency and actually sent out the false alert. This required investigation into the bureaucratic processes that are actually involved in sending out such notifications. It also gave me tremendous, terrifying insight into how fallible these kinds of systems are, and how quickly a single offhand decision can yield a runaway reaction. There were also moments in which research popped up out of necessity. For example, when I needed to determine the best way to acquire a dead person’s DNA for a paternity test, or to understand various bluegrass violin techniques, or to clarify the human pupil’s reaction to opioid use, among others. Falling down these little rabbit holes and emerging with greater knowledge, however random it may be, is one of the greatest pleasures of writing fiction.  KDW: Did you write Seek Immediate Shelter with an outline or a specific order for each character’s chapter in mind? VY: Not really. The idea of a literary experiment really took hold of me from the very beginning, which led to a large amount of trial and error in my writing process. I let each character make his or her own decisions, and then tried to gauge as honestly as possible if their behaviors seemed believably human. There were a lot of false starts and many branching plot points that I pursued and ultimately pruned.  The whole process was a bit like mapping out a completely dark room. I started in the middle, without knowing the shape of the space I was in or its contours or objects. I had no choice, really, but to move and feel my way around. I bumped into many things, but I think every form of discovery begins as a kind of disturbance. After a while I began to feel more confident in my explorations. The real light switch, however, was my editor, Caroline Bleeke. Her guidance and vision for the manuscript was completely illuminating. Once she and I started working together, I knew exactly how to order the stories and unite the characters into a cohesive whole.  9 Books About Living in Parallel Realities Matthew Salesses, yazarı “Disappear Doppelgänger Disappear,” recommends stories about multiple selves Aug 27 – Matthew Salesses Reading Lists KDW: How did the backdrop of Beckitt help sculpt the story or shift the style of prose, if at all? And is the town’s name a direct allusion to a certain canonical existentialist absurdist yazar?  VY: Ha! There was a little bit of intentionality in my choice of the town name, but certainly not enough to put the work in any meaningful dialogue with that of Beckett’s. All I really wanted was to invoke a sense of strangeness even in the everyday. Beckitt was actually based on my own hometown of Longmeadow, which is also located in the Pioneer Valley of Western Massachusetts. After I decided to tell the story through multiple characters, I realized that setting the entire thing in a single community would allow me to believably intertwine their lives and to explore the particular drama that occurs in small, tight-knit communities.  Many people (including some of the characters in the book) assume that towns like Beckitt are perennially quiet and unchanging. One of my goals in sending a false missile alert to its residents was to create enough of an emotional disturbance to reveal the richness of all the lives within it, the vast interiorities of every single resident, living and dead.
