title: Uluslararası Edebiyat Seçkisi: Finding Your Voice as a Woman Writer Raised on Books by Men... (Electric Lit Söyleşileri editoryal arşivinden Türkçeye uyarlanmıştır.)
desc: Julie Buntin and I first met when Electric Literature shared an office with Catapult in the mid-2010s. She was a book editor and the director of Catapult’s beloved educational program; I had recently ...
content:
Julie Buntin and I first met when Electric Literature shared an office with Catapult in the mid-2010s. She was a book editor and the director of Catapult’s beloved educational program; I had recently become Electric Literature’s Executive Director. I was an aspiring yazar with a few short stories; Julie was about to publish her ilk romanı, Marlena, to critical and commercial acclaim. We hit it off as two hard-working, mostly type-A people with the same cynical sense of humor that protects over-eager emotions, and began trading work after we both left the city. Julie to Ann Arbor where she was teaching at the University of Michigan and writing her sophomore novel, Famous Men; me to upstate New York where I was working on my ilk romanı, Slush, which will be published next summer. Julie is my most trusted reader. I have long felt like I can say anything to her; that nothing is too strange, or dark, or vulnerable, or naïve. If I am working out a difficult opinion, she can help me articulate it. What better qualities to have in a writing partner? Famous Men tells the story of Wilhelmina Miles, known as Will, an aspiring şair from the small town of Greening, Michigan. She has long harbored the fantasy that her town’s one success story, the decorated yazar Nathanial Fellow, is her father. When she moves to New York and tracks him down at the MFA program where he teaches, that fantasy deforms into a relationship, one that is financial, professional, sexual, and even a little familial. Famous Men is an entertaining, rich, discomfiting novel that rejects black and white answers to complex questions in favor of subjectivity as its foundational stance. Consent is not a matter of “yes” or “no,” culpability is not an easy verdict, and power is multi-directional. Reading early drafts of Famous Men, I was struck by how they never quite felt like drafts. Scenes were cut, plot points changed, etc., but the world of the novel and the ideas behind it always felt fully formed. Julie has a charismatic prose style that is flowing yet precise, with a clarity of insight that seems casual but is most certainly hard won. When the galley finally arrived, I thought I would dip in and out to gather questions for this interview. But I couldn’t resist reading straight through for a third time; the novel is that compelling and rewarding. Julie and I spoke over video call, with some follow-up over email. I found myself surprisingly nervous to ask her “serious questions” on the record, after so many casual, private conversations. Initial giggling aside, we settled in, and I was grateful to be able to engage with her not as my friend, but as the yazarı one of my favorite kitaplar of this decade. Halimah Marcus: Will, long before she ever meets Nathaniel, reads his work at the library. And because they’re from the same small town, it sparks her imagination about what she could be someday. Who were the yazars that did that for you when you were that age? Julie Buntin: I grew up in Hemingway country. I grew up in the Petoskey area of Northern Michigan where the Nick Adams stories on Walloon Lake are set. Hemingway lived in a lot of places, but there’s a lot of regional Hemingway pride where I’m from in a way I took for granted as a young person—that a small town like that might celebrate their literary grandfather out of pride. My husband’s family is from Lorain, Ohio, where Toni Morrison is from, and he went looking for her house once. There was nothing that said Toni Morrison lived there. Hemingway was a yazar I liked and read at a young age because we had his kitaplar in our house, The Sun Also Rises, For Whom the Bell Tolls, obviously the stories. I wasn’t necessarily thinking, I want to write like this, but I did have this idea of certain yazars as having this cultural impact. I also read a ton of Stephen King, like so much Stephen King. HM: Will internalizes a lot of lessons from being so obsessed with Nathaniel’s work. There’s this great passage about all the women in Nathaniel’s fiction, and the limits of who they could be and the archetypes they represent. Did you internalize any lessons like that from your reading as a young person? JB: With this book, I wrestled a lot with questions I still sit with. I remember reading Herzog by Saul Bellow as a teenager and thinking: This is genius. The high/low voice; it’s so funny. How does he do this? This is everything I could ever want to do as a yazar. And then having a similar reaction to the Rabbit, Run novels by John Updike, loving them without any ability at that age to question the complicated portrayals of women, which are sometimes really reductive. In this book, I was thinking a lot about what happens if part of your formative artistic development involves taking in influences that don’t always make space for your full subjectivity as a person. What happens if those are the models you put ahead of everything else? If the first character you identify with in serious edebiyat is like, a middle-aged man? I was thinking about not only how that would affect you as a yazar, but how it would affect your sense of what kind of woman you wanted to be or could be. We’re so permeable to influence when we’re children and adolescents, especially. I see this with my son, who is five—he reads something and suddenly he’s repeating phrases from it, acting like the characters. That’s something I’m endlessly interested in, so that was floating around in my head for sure: How might there be bleeding between what Will reads and what she thinks? How she presents herself to Nathaniel, how she understands how he might see her—all of that is a creation of her imagination, but also created by the texts of his that she’s read. HM: Later in the book, Will asks Vilma, Nathaniel’s ex and a yazar with acclaim and success, if Vilma was ever afraid that her stories weren’t important or literary enough because they were about all the things women thought and felt. I love this moment, because it’s in a book about everything a woman thought and felt. Did you ever have the feeling that this book isn’t important because it is about a woman? JB: I had that feeling a lot when I was writing my first book [Marlena]. When I started writing it in my MFA, I remember getting a lot of feedback that boiled down to things like, why do we care about what teenage girls are doing? There were obviously other problems with the early drafts, but there was often a question of, is this YA? YA is wonderful—I would love to write it sometime—but that question wasn’t a question. It was a way of saying that the material doesn’t feel high stakes because of what it’s about. For example, I remember learning about Who Will Run the Frog Hospital [by Lorrie Moore] in grad school, and it being presented as a kind of failed novel, where the girlhood sections were dragging down this more interesting potent story of an adult relationship, and thinking, when I finally read it, girlhood is the point of this book. HM: One of the culminations of Famous Men happens during the height of the #MeToo movement, when the Harvey Weinstein news is breaking. At the time, pretty much immediately, people started talking about #MeToo novels, even applying the term to novels that were written before—novels that embodied the values of the #MeToo movement, in terms of believing women or the value of consent and autonomy, novels that were expressing often painful stories of sexual violence and abuses of power. Famous Men engages deeply with those themes. But reading that part of the book, I thought about how this novel is a document of #MeToo and everything that led up to it, even more than a “#MeToo novel.” Because it all started 10 years ago, which makes it practically historical fiction. What’s your relationship with that term today? How do you feel it’s changed over time: in the last 10 years, and while writing this novel? JB: This book took me many years to write. I started it in the summer of 2019, which I remember as a moment of almost hopefulness. There was some sense of a public reckoning having happened, and of justice or change that was going to be lasting and positive. Maybe I’m just too optimistic in general, but I was like, okay, this is hard but what will come out of it is a slightly better world. When I started writing in my MFA, I remember getting a lot of feedback that boiled down to, why do we care about what teenage girls are doing? I finished the book last year. And now we’re in a time when there are even scarier questions to ask: Was any progress real? Has the backlash to #MeToo actually undone the positive things about #MeToo? What was that? Was #MeToo just another version of something that’s happened over and over, and now we’re in a more regressive place? I had children during that time. My son was born in 2021, when I was still kind of hoping for some sort of brighter future. My daughter was born in 2024, and I fear she’ll have less rights and protections than I have. When #MeToo happened, there was a sense that what was publicly condoned three months ago is no longer okay. Of a real turning point. And I thought, what would it be like to tell this story from the perspective of a character who can’t inhabit that shift because of various things that are happening in her life? HM: Because she feels implicated. JB: She feels implicated and she feels stuck. She’s implicated because of the choices she’s made. She’s implicated because of her relationship with this person [Nathaniel], which is financial. She’s financially dependent on him, but she also loves him. I say love, not even in a sexual or romantic way; it’s almost like a friendship by the end of the book. HM: I love how Will and Nathaniel’s first encounters, at a reading she attends and then in his office, set up the dynamics of their future relationship. She acts in surprising ways. He probably acts more predictably, in terms of what we might expect a guy like that to do. At the reading, he’s goes to help her carry chairs, and he touches her leg. She thinks it’s the wrong kind of first touch. In their second meeting, she’s at his office and drops a book, and when she goes to pick it up, she pushes it further under the table, and then ties his shoe. The moment is so surprising to everyone involved, including the reader. JB: Including her. HM: The gesture is at once submissive in kind of a sexual way, and also infantilizing to him. The way I read it, when he touches her leg, she’s learning what he expects from her. And then when she ties his shoe, she’s delivering on what he expects. She’s one step ahead. Where does that kind of intuition come from? JB: It’s every story she’s internalized and read. She knows Nathaniel’s work really well. She knows the kind of move he might respond to. And when she has that moment with him at the reading, she realizes something about what character she would be to him. Once she knows what character she would be to him, she understands how to get his attention. She’s a character who kind of wants his attention no matter what, even after she realizes that he’s not the person that she thought he was. She has come there for him, or because of a vision of life that his work offered her. It’s parasocial. It’s a fantasy. But once she’s there, she is intoxicated by this world that she sees at this reading. Moving to New York alone at a young age can make anybody kind of bananas. She doesn’t have anyone. She doesn’t have any friends. She’s on her own. So the step that is crucial to that moment is knowing his work as well as she does, and having this instinct about what Nathaniel might respond to. This is a way of getting at some of these questions about the male gaze and how the pressure of it over the course of a lifetime can make you act in ways that feel as if they are not coming from your true, essential self. Or that you’re being steered by something outside of you, which is an experience I certainly felt as a young woman. Who am I doing this for? What norm am I trying to satisfy with this? Who am I trying to satisfy? HM: From the first chapter, Will breaks one of Nathaniel’s rules, which is: If you need the past to tell a story, you’re telling the wrong story. The book begins in her small town of Greening and deals a lot with the way she experiences the male gaze. She gets negative attention from the boys in her school because she has big boobs, and she feels like her mother’s boyfriend is always watching her. I wonder if there’s actually something feminist about including the past in this way. I’m interested in passivity in fiction, and passivity in women. JB: I hope that that is how it’s read. You might get through this whole book and be like, Will makes bad decisions, she’s an imperfect character in all of these ways, she doesn’t learn anything, and she doesn’t grow. She compromises left and right; what kind of vision of feminism is this? Is this feminist? You could absolutely have that reaction. The way Will tells her story, and the choices she makes about when to break the rules she has been taught are givens, is an act of agency. A declaration of, “I no longer adhere to this narrative that trapped me for so long” and “I will not tell it the way he would teach me to.” A lot of those choices were happening on a structural level, like when and where to start the story, or to cut. HM: Some readers might be frustrated with Will for her perceived passivity. There’s so much that happens with Nathaniel that she feels is a foregone conclusion, probably because she’s anticipating his expectations. She’s dictating her own fate while also feeling like it’s pre-written. How is that a strength for her and how is it a liability? JB: We all have these things as yazars that creep in, book to book or project to project. I’m interested in passivity in fiction, and passivity in women. One true thing about how I have experienced the world that I’ve not always been able to find in edebiyat is: What does it mean to be socialized in every way to make things easier for other people, to be helpful, to be accommodating of everyone at the expense of yourself, to not cause a ruckus? I was raised in that mold, and so much of my experience of coming of age has been about dealing with those impulses in myself in every context and trying to figure out when they serve me and when they don’t. Will is incredibly self-determined and she’s not passive at all until she gets stuck in a system where the power is so out of whack that she can’t get it back. She gets in over her head when she’s really young and then she’s swept up in this wave and she’s really stuck. There’s this feeling of time running away from her and “how did I get here?” and “this thing has its own velocity and I’m trapped in it,” which was a way of writing about passivity, and trying to write realistically about those times where you have more self-awareness about what’s going on then you have ability to change it. HM: Or the will to change it. JB: I was interested in there being a kind of weird aggressive agency in not acknowledging the truth, in lying to yourself a lot and really hard, and in the ways that you have to lie to yourself if you are opting into certain kinds of relationships that harm yourself or others. A certain amount of self-deception becomes a matter of course, in those contexts. HM: The violence in Famous Men is very grayed or obscured or sometimes blacked-out, forgotten or confusing to the person who experienced it. The violence in the book that Will writes, the novel within the novel, is very literalized. JB: That was a really deliberate, conscious choice. You’re not always awake to this in the drafting of a book, but it became more evident to me as I wrote. Especially after I had a first draft. [I wanted to explore] the kinds of violence that are in some way muffled, that might be especially hard for a young woman to define. I have a very clear interpretation of the things that happen to Will as a girl, and where they fall on the violation scale. But Will doesn’t, because of the ways that she’s been raised and the context in which these things happened, and the failure of certain frameworks to protect her, even within her own family. I was thinking there about what we demand of a victim, or what we need women’s stories to look like in order to feel satisfied that they truly have experienced harm. Nathaniel gives Will the advice to write something from her life that she can’t stop thinking about. But when she does that, fictionalizing this murky experience she had as a teenager, he tells her to escalate it. I was thinking there about what we demand of a victim, or what we need women’s stories to look like in order to feel satisfied that they truly have experienced harm. We want to know what exactly happened. We need them to look a certain way. I remember taking a cab home from the airport around the time of the Kavanaugh hearings, and the driver brought it up and kept asking, “But how did she get to the second floor?” It was awful. And why is that? What is unsatisfying about the mess and the confusion and the murk and the ways that all of those things can have years of fallout, and complicated intersections with other kinds of harm that happen later? HM: Nathaniel reads every draft of Will’s book, he gives her notes, he pushes her towards a bigger plot, essentially leading Will away from herself. But she calls him a good teacher, directly and in various ways throughout. In your opinion, is Nathaniel a good teacher? JB: I think he is in some ways. You can’t spend six years writing a character and not develop some sympathy. I was inhabiting Will’s point of view, but I have a sense of him outside of that point of view too. I see him as a teacher who is not in his prime anymore. He’s tired, he’s teaching the same shit he’s always taught, he’s not doing anything new in class, he’s regurgitating old lessons. But even his autopilot has moments of profundity that a young yazar might be able to latch onto in a way that would be instructive or useful. I do think of him as someone who is interested in his students for personal reasons, but he’s also interested in in their work; at least when it aligns with his taste. That’s the complicated thing about these charismatic teacher figures; sometimes good teachers are good teachers for certain students or for certain kinds of work, or they are good teacher for a minute and then terrible after that, or the longing for their approval outshines any other aspect of what you may or may not learn from them. HM: As a fiction yazar, why did you make the characters şairs first? 7 Novels About Toxic Student-Teacher Relationships Mentorship in these kitaplar teeter between nurturing and manipulative Aug 8 – Lauren Aliza Green Reading Lists JB: There’s something really pure and beautiful to me about şairry. The stakes are incredibly high on a human scale and incredibly low in other ways. There was something about that scale that was really interesting. Poetry was the first art form I really loved, which is probably in part what this book is talking to. Louise Glück, Elizabeth Bishop, specifically that Elizabeth Bishop poem “In the Waiting Room,” where she has that line where she’s like, why should I be myself? [“Why should I be my aunt, or me, or anyone?”] I remember reading that as a teenager and thinking, this is the ultimate question that one could spend all of life pursuing.   The post Finding Your Voice as a Woman Writer Raised on Books by Men appeared first on Electric Literature.

content:
When my husband and I started house hunting in the DC suburbs three years ago, it never crossed our minds that we’d live as anything but a typical nuclear family: just us and our future kids. But the house we bought featured an apartment-style basement, complete with its own kitchen, full bathroom, and private entrance. The month we bought it, a friend of ours lost his apartment. “I’ll rent yours for a few months, tops,” he said. He lived with us for two years.  I got attached to the extra company, and the extra income. We recently welcomed a new tenant—a stranger, for the first time. But within weeks, she became a staple in our daughter’s life, bringing her fruit from the farmers markets where she works, delighting as my toddler gobbles it up or puckers in disapproval. A lot of stories in Living, Together, start somewhere like this—at the crossroads of need, opportunity, and flexibility. It’s an anthology about living communally, and editor Samantha Paige Rosen uses the term very broadly. The essays and Q&As cover roommates and group houses, but also traditional Native American communal living and a yazars’ residency held at a couple’s home in Los Angeles, to name just a couple examples.  As different as the living scenarios are, I was most struck by what the essays have in common. By making the deliberate choice to share space intimately, in ways that are unconventional by our modern Western standards, each contributor is essentially seeding community into their lives. And throughout the pages, acts of tenderness and generosity spring up like wildflowers—people caring for aging parents, others helping to raise children that aren’t their own. The resulting book is a rare read: one that’s unflinchingly honest about our current world (including the financial inequities and hardships that often drive people to live communally), but that will also leave you feeling hopeful for the future. I spoke over Zoom with Rosen and two of her contributors. Adam Vitcavage, founder of Debutiful, lived with his sister for four years in his 20s. Suanne Carlson is the co-founder of the Homes on Wheels Alliance, a nonprofit dedicated to supporting fellow nomads who live on the road.  Emily Mirengoff: In your introduction, you quote Margot Kahn, saying that an anthology is a “town hall bound in pages.” For all their virtues, town halls can get bogged down by a few loud voices with limited perspectives. But the scope in Living, Together is breathtaking. How did you ensure that you were covering a broad base of voices, experiences, and ideas? Samantha Paige Rosen: Honestly, the main challenge was narrowing down the number of voices and living scenarios. It felt very important that I wasn’t representing just a few specific life experiences, or one income level, or one or two geographical regions. I’m glad you think it’s broad enough—part of me still feels like it should cover even more. My wonderful agent had to rein me in and advised me to put the individual and story first, rather than the living scenario. EM: You describe your hope that this book will help us pause, reflect, plan, and act toward a future that is more than just living, but offers sustainable resiliency for the future. Can you share your favorite example(s) of communal living offering that flexibility and resilience? Not only is our way of living tied up in capitalism and industrialization, but it’s also rooted in colonialism. SPR: It’s impossible to pick a favorite—Suanne would certainly be one, although I’ll let her share her story—but two examples come to mind. Hope Meadows is an intergenerational neighborhood in Illinois that was founded 30 years ago on a former Air Force base. Initially, it offered free housing and benefits to those who permanently adopted kids out of foster care and reduced-cost housing to seniors who would volunteer within the community and wanted to be involved in the kids’ lives, like surrogate grandparents. When it began in the mid-90s, it was the first of its kind in the US, and it was incredibly successful. But over time, the number of children in foster care dropped significantly, which of course was a good thing, and it no longer made sense for Hope Meadows to pursue their foster care license and future adoption services, and they lost the associated grant that helped them cover the free and reduced-cost housing.  They realized that they had to pivot to be more of a general intergenerational community that provides low-cost, but no longer free, housing. For Living, Together, I spoke with the first-ever senior resident, Fran Biederman, and Hank Gamel, the current executive director. He’s always coming up with innovative ideas that keep the intergenerational mission alive while trying to address financial needs—like partnering with Habitat for Humanity to pair local high school students interested in learning trade skills with community members whose houses need repairs. Hope Meadows may not look exactly like it did 25 years ago, but that doesn’t mean there’s not still a benefit to the community, as Fran attests to.  Another example is Simone Gorrindo’s essay about her early years as a military wife. She describes moving as a newlywed from New York City to rural Georgia, not even knowing how to drive, when her husband deployed almost immediately. Across the street, her new neighbor Rachel was going through the same thing—but while Simone’s natural response to loneliness was to turn further inward, Rachel’s was to turn outward, to connect with others as a means of resilience. They became incredibly close and were able to survive some major life moments without their spouses by leaning on each other. You might define that more as neighboring than communal living, but it’s the same mindset in my eyes.  EM: I love the way your book does this—it widens the definition of communal living to encompass not just living under a single roof, but the act of building meaningful and intentional community. That reminds me a lot of your essay, Suanne, about your experience as a nomad. Suanne Carlson: Yes, not only are nomads not under the same roof, but we often live thousands of miles apart, and may see each other once or twice a year at gatherings—but we’re still in community. EM: You describe caravanning in community with your fellow nomads. Gathering in this way reminds me of how humankind lived for millennia. Of course, that’s much less common now. What do you think has been lost and gained in that change? Because we’re living an alternative lifestyle that many don’t understand, there’s a sort of us-against-the-world connection. SC: It’s true, our ancestors were nomads. By necessity, they followed the weather, they followed food. I personally feel like there’s some genetic code within me that still thinks it’s a necessity. Of course, as soon as we started corralling animals for food, growing and cultivating plants, that required a stable location—which eventually led to manufacturing and the workforce that’s needed for it.  But when I go through large cities now, that’s where my mind goes: “Oh, this is the local workforce.” Not, “Oh, this is the local community.” Our society’s way of life feels like it’s designed to sustain an economy, not a community.  SPR: I’m glad Suanne made that point. Not only is our way of living tied up in capitalism and industrialization, but it’s also rooted in colonialism. In Living, Together, Rodney Bordeaux, former president of the Rosebud Sioux Tribe in South Dakota, üzerine konuşuyor: the impact of the federal policies that ended their nomadic way of life, forced assimilation, and sent Native kids to boarding schools away from their people. The loss of freedom and land and means, but also of community—of connection and identity—is still so deeply felt.  EM: I think a lot of people—including me, before I read your Q&A—would guess that living in your car would be lonely. But you say you feel a stronger sense of community now than you did living in the conventional neighborhood. Why is that? SC: I’m an introvert. I like to camp alone with others who like to camp alone. That’s true socially, but also for safety, because I like to camp in the back country, in nature.  The thing about nomads is that when we get together, we know we’ll only have a specific amount of time together—a week, a night. We get down to the nitty-gritty, important stuff right away. There’s very little small talk. And that builds a connection, a sense of like-mindedness that I had not ever experienced before. Also, because we’re living an alternative lifestyle that many don’t understand, there’s a sort of us-against-the-world connection. EM: What is the most misunderstood aspect of this lifestyle? SC: People only know what they know and what they see. And since people live in towns and cities, the vehicle-dwellers that they see are those on the street—who certainly count among our population of vehicle-dwellers, but they’re not nomads. Because we’re not usually in cities, nomads can seem invisible. But I would love for people to understand that we value the communities we visit, we support them economically, and we love and treasure the public lands—we do not leave a trace. In fact, we often pick up after people who do leave a trace. Another thing people don’t realize is that living in your vehicle requires learning a really specific skillset. Living in a vehicle is simple, but not easy. And transitioning from a sticks and bricks to a vehicle is a major change. For that reason, the Homes on Wheels Alliance has mentoring camps, where we pair experienced nomads with brand new nomads and help them learn how to make that transition.  SPR: I love that you mention mentoring, because that’s related to what I was trying to accomplish with this book. Living, Together isn’t a how-to book, but I wanted people who are curious about communal living for whatever reason to be guided through different possibilities by those who’ve experienced them.  EM: One of the more classic communal living scenarios is, of course, roommates. Adam, in your essay about your sister, you wrote, “We never liked each other growing up and fought more than I think most siblings do.” Yet you chose to live together as adults. What is it about sibling relationships that creates this unique push-pull dynamic? Adam Vitcavage: When you’re a kid, you don’t really appreciate your sibling—they’re just someone you’re stuck with. My relationship with my sister wasn’t toxic when we were kids, but it was volatile. But I think that, when push comes to shove, most people will have their family’s back. And with siblings, the older you get, the more you realize you have in common, and how much you care about each other. There’s a shared bond—whether it’s trauma or happiness—and a shorthand language that is specific to only your relationship.  When it comes to living situations, I believe anything is possible, nothing is forever, and we’ll always land on our feet. SPR: There’s a great line in your piece that speaks to this: “Living with you, I was able to be more than the typical considerate roommate—I was able to be myself.” AV: My sister and I, we grew up and learned to wear masks. I think we all do—everyone hides things. She got married young and lived with her husband all through her 20s, and I lived with roommates. But after her divorce, when we moved in together, we realized we could really be ourselves—even the worst versions of ourselves. Earlier, we talked about loneliness, which is related. Nowadays, most of us are living this editorialized life on the internet. We only post the happy memories, or the best photos. But 2016 was the worst year of my life, and if I’d had a girlfriend or a roommate, I would have hidden things. Instead, it was beneficial because my sister could see me at my worst, and she understood everything.  EM: You currently own a home with your wife and are expecting a baby soon. What is your relationship with your sister like these days? How do you feel like that roommate era reshaped it? AV: My sister and I are both “out of sight, out of mind” people. I live in Denver, and she’s in Phoenix. But we send each other memes every day, and it’s important to us. Laughing at the same things is our love language. And if she ever needs a place to live, she knows she’s very welcome anytime. There’s also a chance my mom will move in with us. When it comes to living situations, I believe anything is possible, nothing is forever, and we’ll always land on our feet. EM: So many essays in the book say something along those lines: “I’m not committing to communal living forever, or maybe I’ll do it again in another form someday, we’ll see what the future holds.” But nearly every contributor discusses that willingness to embrace change, and the unfamiliar.  SC: That definitely applies to the nomadic lifestyle, too—flexibility is baked in. When one of my friends needed an operation, she stayed on part of her kid’s property. I have another friend who stayed put for a while to care for his aging father.  For myself, as I age, reality dictates that I probably won’t be able to keep traveling in my car as I do now. So, this past fall, I decided to find a home base. Another good friend of mine needed to get off the road because of medical issues, so she’s my housemate while I stay on the road. In the meantime, I’ll keep traveling most of the year until I can’t anymore. Literature’s Great Alternative Families Jun 26 – Victoria Redel Reading Lists SPR: Working on this book absolutely helped me see living situations in a more flexible light. I lived with my parents starting in my late 20s for six years—that’s what inspired me to write this book—but for the past year, I’ve lived alone in a townhouse, although they’re across the street. I think about bringing in a roommate, or living in a more deliberately communal setting. But I have the same concerns that many people have—around geography, finances, and interpersonal challenges. That’s why I told Living, Together’s essayists not to hold anything back. Communal living isn’t always easy, but I hope that, when people see more of a full picture in this book, they’ll decide it might be worth the risk. We’re all a little afraid of taking a leap and having things not work out to our satisfaction. But when we live that way, we end up depriving ourselves of amazing opportunities.
